notes: Agent hook journeys. These cover hooks as an agent capability -- whether a declared hook runs and what its output reaches -- rather than the listing that shows them, which is a panel and lives with the panels. The effect a user depends on is asserted through the request body, by scripting a turn that answers only when the hook's stdout is present and pairing it with one that answers only when it is absent, so a dropped hook renders a named string instead of timing out. Each sentinel is arithmetic the shell resolves, so the matched literal exists nowhere in the agent config that declares the hook -- only in what the hook printed. One journey per hook, because a turn can require one body substring and these need to fail separately to say which hook was dropped.

scenarios.name: A session-start hook's output is in the request the model receives
scenarios.description: An agentSpawn hook that prints a sentinel -- asserts the sentinel is present in the request body the agent sends, which is the only place a session-start hook's effect can be observed
steps: prompt:answer once the spawn hook has run
scenarios.observe: A session-start hook runs once, before any prompt, so its output has to survive until the first request or it is lost -- and nothing on screen would say so either way. The answering turn is matched on the request body containing the hook's stdout; the paired turn requires that same output absent, so it cannot fire for any other reason, and whichever fires names the outcome on screen. This is the hook whose output has the furthest to travel, which is what makes it worth asserting separately from the per-prompt one.

match.userInputContains: answer once the spawn hook has run
answer once the spawn hook has run

scenarios.name: A per-prompt hook's output is in the request the model receives
scenarios.description: A userPromptSubmit hook that prints a sentinel -- asserts the sentinel is present in the request body the agent sends, which is the only place a context hook's effect can be observed
steps: prompt:answer once the prompt hook has run
scenarios.observe: A context hook exists to put something in front of the model, and no panel can show whether it did. The answering turn is matched on the request body containing the hook's stdout, so it can only fire if the hook ran and its output was injected; the paired turn requires that same output absent, which turns a silently dropped hook into a named string rather than a timeout. Both name this prompt and both are sticky, so a background call can neither consume the positive nor be answered by either.

match.userInputContains: answer once the prompt hook has run
answer once the prompt hook has run

scenarios.name: A pre-tool hook that refuses stops the tool from running
scenarios.description: A preToolUse hook matched to the file-read tool that exits non-zero -- asserts the tool is reported as failed rather than executed, and the turn continues afterwards
scenarios.observe: A pre-tool hook is the one hook that can stop an action, and this pins that it does: the call is reported failed and the model still gets its turn, so a refusal neither runs the tool nor wedges the session. The follow-up turn is matched on the request carrying a tool result, so it can only answer the continuation of the refused call -- a refusal that ended the turn outright leaves it unanswered. The refusal also preempts the approval gate entirely: this same read asks for approval when the matcher does not name it, and here no gate ever appears, so the hook is consulted before the user is. Known gap this deliberately does not assert: the hook's own stderr never reaches the screen, so the card says only 'Tool execution failed' and a user cannot see which hook refused or why. Asserting the reason would fail today; asserting its absence would fail once it is surfaced.

scenarios.name: A pre-tool hook matched to another tool leaves this one alone
scenarios.description: The same refusing preToolUse hook, matched to a tool the turn never calls -- asserts the call it does make runs normally, so the refusal is scoped by the matcher rather than applied to everything
steps: prompt:read the manifest with a scoped hook
scenarios.observe: This is the control for the refusal journey, and without it a hook engine that refused every tool would pass that one. The hook is identical and still exits non-zero; only its matcher differs, naming a tool this turn never calls. The read therefore reaches its approval gate and completes once approved, which the absent failure text checks -- the same string the refusal journey asserts present, so the two together attribute the outcome to the matcher rather than to the hook merely existing. That the gate appears at all is the other half: a refused call never reaches it.

match.userInputContains: read the manifest with a scoped hook
